title: Understanding the Experience of the Visually Impaired towards a Multi-Sensorial Architectural Design
research_focus: To holistically understand the world of the visually impaired, extract the qualities of space that accommodate their needs, and show the importance of multi-sensory, holistic designs for the blind, critically condemning the dominance of the visual modality in current architectural practice.

sample_context.description: The study synthesized experiences from multiple sources: written statements from blind architect Chris Downey (lost sight at 45), written accounts from John Hull (Emeritus Professor, blind), a semi-structured interview with A. A. (a 24-year-old Egyptian, blind for 18 years, now sighted), and participant observation of 5 visually impaired children (ages 3-8) at an NGO in Cairo, Egypt.
sample_context.setting: Various built environments including airports, Bauhaus University, Old Cairo streets, a park, and an NGO classroom setting.

findings.consequent: Perception of spatial characteristics (e.g., proximity to openings, movement)
findings.description: Visually impaired individuals perceive airflow on their skin, which helps them identify the presence of openings (like doors and windows) and understand the movement of air within a space.

findings.consequent: Identification of window locations and light intensity
findings.description: The sensation of heat from sunlight on the skin allows visually impaired individuals to locate windows and infer the intensity of light in a space without direct visual input.

findings.antecedent: Smell of natural elements (perfumes, incenses, bakeries, coffee, fresh flowers, water, soil, rocks)
findings.consequent: Spatial recognition and memory of specific areas
findings.description: Distinct natural and artificial scents in an environment serve as important cues for visually impaired people to recognize and remember specific locations, contributing to their mental map of the surroundings.
supporting_quotes: The scent along the walk was important as participants remembered specific areas through the smell of perfumes, incenses, bakeries and coffee.

smell of fresh flowers and water was strong, felt like the smell of freshness. The special smell of water stream blending in with the soil and rocks, splashing on the rocks then to our skin felt like a way of blending in with the natural elements in the park.

findings.antecedent: Atmosphere and activities (breezes, sounds of leaves, birds, street life)
findings.consequent: Perception of environmental dynamism and liveliness
findings.description: The presence of various natural sounds and ambient activity contributes to the perception of an environment as dynamic and lively, contrasting with 'dead' or 'flat' spaces lacking such sensory input.
supporting_quotes: The outside is so much more dynamic. There are breezes, there are the sounds of a breeze through the leaves in the trees, or birds off in the distance. I spend a lot of time on the front porch of our house, enjoying the street life and all the sounds. There's a dynamic to the environment outside that is often excluded from the interior.

findings.antecedent: Material texture (roughness, smoothness, hard, soft, carpeted, wood, concrete, asphalt, pavers)
findings.consequent: Material identification, spatial navigation, and comfort
findings.description: Visually impaired individuals use active touch (cane, feet, hands) to perceive the texture of materials, which aids in identifying surfaces, navigating spaces, and influencing comfort levels (e.g., rough pavers causing fatigue).
supporting_quotes: I test materials with my cane to see how they feel.
A contrast between two materials should be clear in its texture.
Rough pavers were harder to walk on, so after a while they had to sit and rest from walking.

findings.consequent: Material identification and perception of environmental qualities
findings.description: The temperature of materials (e.g., cold wood) provides additional haptic information that contributes to the identification of materials and the overall perception of the environment.
supporting_quotes: The smooth and cold feel of the old wood was dominant.

findings.consequent: Object recognition, understanding of size and scale
findings.description: Visually impaired individuals, especially children, learn to recognize the size and shape of objects through active haptic exploration (e.g., play dough, arranging forms on a rod), which is crucial for developing a mental representation of their surroundings.
supporting_quotes: Stereognosis is developed to train visually impaired children to perceive the size and shape of objects through their hands.
The children learn to understand that there are different forms of objects... visually impaired children touch and feel the objects to be able to recognize them.

findings.consequent: Object identification and confirmation of mental images
findings.description: The act of touching and feeling objects allows visually impaired individuals to identify their attributes and properties, confirming their mental images of these objects, even after regaining sight.
supporting_quotes: I could feel the attributes of any object by touching and feeling it. When I saw the table, I knew that this was a table because I remember touching and feeling it, just like seeing it.

findings.antecedent: Ground topography and contours (floor textures, changes in surface)
findings.consequent: Perception of spatial characteristics and navigation cues
findings.description: Perceiving the contours and textures of the ground through active tactile exploration (feet, cane) provides critical information for understanding the spatial layout and navigating the environment.
supporting_quotes: perceiving the contours of the ground underneath were considered active tactile stimulants.
The participants focused on the floor textures under their feet and how it changes the perception when it changes.

findings.consequent: Perception of space wideness, crowdedness, and ceiling height
findings.description: The characteristics of sound echo (e.g., high echo for wide/empty spaces, low for narrow/crowded, intermediate for preferred ceiling heights) are crucial for visually impaired individuals to understand the dimensions and occupancy of a space.
supporting_quotes: Echo used to play a very important role in understanding the surrounding space, it made me understand the space wideness and how crowded it is, high echo means a space is wide and empty and vice versa. I usually prefer ceilings with intermediate heights, low ceilings result in high echoes, while high ceilings make it hard to track echo.

findings.consequent: Development of mental maps and spatial understanding
findings.description: Integrating information from touch (cane, hands, feet), sound (echo, objects), and smell allows visually impaired individuals to construct a comprehensive mental map of their surroundings, facilitating identification and navigation of places.
supporting_quotes: To be able to identify and understand a place, I walk around, touch the surroundings with my cane, hands and feet, hit several objects while walking, clap to feel the echo, and thus, the wideness of space, and I smell the materials and this is how I develop a mental map of the surroundings, making it easier to understand the place when revisited.

findings.consequent: Recognition of familiar environments and specific locations
findings.description: Specific aural, olfactory, and haptic experiences (e.g., unique street sounds, distinct smells, recognizable material textures) enable visually impaired individuals to recognize and differentiate familiar places.
supporting_quotes: some participants recognized the street due to its aural experience only.
Places were easily identified with smell because every place has a certain smell that can be recalled when revisited.

findings.description: A harmonious integration of haptic, auditory, and olfactory perceptions is essential for visually impaired individuals to build accurate cognitive maps, enabling successful orientation and mobility in familiar environments.
supporting_quotes: For successful orientation and mobility of the visually impaired, a harmony between haptic, auditory and olfactory perceptions is achieved and that is how they easily recognize familiar environments, the senses synchronization.

derived_hypotheses: Haptic and aural inclusive designs are essential to create environments suitable for the visually impaired to empower them towards an independent, safe and efficient life.
Designing visual borders with tactile qualities and clear material texture contrasts can improve spatial understanding for the visually impaired.
mechanism_candidates: Mental map formation (integration of multi-sensory information)
Senses synchronization (harmony between haptic, auditory, and olfactory perceptions)
Active and passive touch (distinct haptic feedback mechanisms)
transferability_limits: Findings may be influenced by the specific cultural context of Cairo, Egypt, particularly regarding olfactory cues (e.g., specific perfumes, incenses, bakeries).

The experiences of individuals who lost sight later in life (Downey) may differ from those blind from birth or early childhood (A.A., children), potentially limiting generalizability across different blindness onset types.
The reliance on self-reported experiences and observations in specific settings may not fully capture the diversity of visually impaired experiences globally.
limitations: The study relies on a synthesis of existing literature and a small number of direct participants, which may limit the depth and breadth of new empirical data.
The specific cultural and environmental context (Cairo, Egypt) for some participants may introduce unique factors not generalizable to all visually impaired populations.
The paper does not explicitly discuss the potential for individual differences in sensory processing or adaptation among visually impaired individuals.
